passages.happening: Jesus tells his followers that some of them will see the kingdom of God come with power before they die. Six days later he takes Peter, James, and John up a high mountain, away from everyone. There his appearance changes before their eyes. His clothes shine whiter than any cloth could ever be washed. Elijah and Moses appear and talk with him. Peter, terrified and not knowing what to say, offers to build three shelters. Then a cloud covers them, and a voice speaks from it: “This is My beloved Son. Listen to Him!” Suddenly the two visitors are gone, and only Jesus is there.
passages.hearers:
Just before this, Jesus has said he must suffer and die (8:31). Now three disciples see who he really is. The word 'transfigured' means changed in form. For a moment the glory that was hidden in Jesus shows through.

Mark says the clothes were whiter than any launderer could bleach them. A launderer, or fuller, was a tradesman who washed and whitened new cloth. Everyone knew how white a good fuller could get a cloak. This was whiter than that. It was not of this world.

The shelters Peter wants to build were booths, the kind of simple huts Israel lived in each autumn at the Feast of Tabernacles to remember the years in the desert (Leviticus 23:42-43). Peter may want to make the moment last, or to honour all three men. Mark simply says he did not know what to say.

Mark does not name the mountain. Since the 200s Christians have pointed to Mount Tabor in Galilee. Many modern scholars suggest Mount Hermon, the great mountain near Caesarea Philippi, where Jesus was in the last chapter. No one can be sure.
passages.ot:
Almost every detail looks back to Moses on Mount Sinai. There too a cloud covered the mountain: “For six days the cloud covered it, and on the seventh day the LORD called to Moses from within the cloud” (Exodus 24:16). Moses' face shone after he spoke with God (Exodus 34:29). In Daniel's vision God's clothing was “white as snow” (Daniel 7:9).

Moses and Elijah both met God on a mountain, and both left this world in an unusual way. Elijah went up “into heaven in a whirlwind” (2 Kings 2:11), and of Moses Scripture says “no one to this day knows the location of his grave” (Deuteronomy 34:6). Many read them as standing for the Law and the Prophets.

The voice's last words, 'Listen to him', echo Moses' promise that God would raise up a prophet like him: “You must listen to him” (Deuteronomy 18:15).
passages.hard: What did Jesus mean in verse 1, that some would see the kingdom come with power before they died? If he meant the end of the world, it did not happen in their lifetime, and some readers take that as a mistake. Others read it as pointing to what follows at once: three of them see his glory on the mountain six days later. Others point to his rising from the dead and the coming of the Spirit, when the kingdom came with power. Christians have held each of these views. Mark's placing of the saying right before the mountain suggests he saw at least a first answer there.
passages.asks: The voice does not say 'Build him a shelter' or 'Look at him'. It says 'Listen to him.' The glory is meant to make the disciples trust the hard words Jesus has just spoken about the cross. Ask whether you want Jesus' glory more than his words, and what he has said that you would rather not hear.

passages.happening: On the way down, Jesus tells the three to tell no one what they saw until the Son of Man has risen from the dead. They keep quiet, but they puzzle over what 'rising from the dead' means. Then they ask him why the scribes say Elijah must come first. Jesus says Elijah does come first and restores all things. But he adds that the Son of Man must suffer, and that Elijah has already come, and people did to him whatever they wanted.
passages.hearers:
Many Jews in Jesus' day believed in a resurrection, but they expected it at the end of the age. Martha says of her dead brother, “I know that he will rise again in the resurrection at the last day” (John 11:24). The idea that one man would rise from the dead ahead of everyone else made no sense to the disciples.

The question about Elijah came from the last words of the Old Testament prophets. God promised, “Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and awesome Day of the LORD” (Malachi 4:5). An older Jewish book, the Wisdom of Ben Sira, says Elijah is ready to turn the hearts of fathers to their sons and to restore the tribes of Jacob. So people were waiting for Elijah. If Jesus was the Messiah, the disciples wondered, where was Elijah?

Jesus' answer is that Elijah has come, in John the Baptist. John dressed like Elijah (1:6). And as Elijah was hunted by Queen Jezebel, John was killed at the wish of Herodias (6:17-29).
passages.ot: Malachi said Elijah “will turn the hearts of the fathers to their children” (Malachi 4:6). Jesus joins this to another strand of Scripture: the Son of Man “must suffer many things and be rejected,” as Isaiah's suffering servant was “despised and rejected by men” (Isaiah 53:3). Glory and suffering both belong to the plan.
passages.asks: The disciples had just seen glory and wanted to talk about prophecy charts. Jesus keeps bringing them back to the cross. Ask whether your interest in the Bible's big questions ever becomes a way of avoiding what it asks of you today.

passages.t: I do believe; help my unbelief
passages.happening: At the foot of the mountain there is a commotion. The other disciples have failed to help a boy, and scribes are arguing with them. The boy's father explains. A spirit has made his son unable to speak. It throws him to the ground, he foams at the mouth, grinds his teeth, and goes stiff. It has thrown him into fire and water. The father says, “But if You can do anything, have compassion on us and help us.” Jesus answers, “If You can?” and, “All things are possible to him who believes!” The father cries out, “I do believe; help my unbelief!” Jesus commands the spirit to leave. The boy goes still like a corpse, and people say he is dead. But Jesus takes his hand and raises him up. Later the disciples ask why they could not drive it out. Jesus says, “This kind cannot come out, except by prayer.”
passages.hearers:
The boy's signs are much like what we now call epilepsy, a condition of the brain that causes seizures. Ancient people knew these signs well. A Greek medical writing from about 400 BC, On the Sacred Disease, argued that seizures have natural causes like any other illness. Matthew, telling the same story, says the boy “has seizures” (Matthew 17:15). Mark tells it as a case of an evil spirit, and Jesus speaks to the spirit directly. Elsewhere Mark keeps illness and possession apart (1:32-34).

Think of what the father had lived through. 'From childhood', he says. For years he had pulled his son out of fires and out of water. He had come for help and the disciples had failed. No wonder his faith is shaky.

The way the boy is raised echoes other stories. Jesus 'took him by the hand' and he 'stood up', the same words Mark uses when Jesus raised Jairus's daughter (5:41-42), and close to the words of Jesus' own rising.
passages.ot: Jesus' cry, 'O unbelieving generation', sounds like Moses coming down from Sinai to find the people faithless at the foot of the mountain (Exodus 32). The pattern repeats: glory above, failure below.
passages.hard:
Does this story mean that seizures, or illness of the mind, are caused by demons? Christians hold that evil is real, and the Gospels tell of real possession. But most Christians today hold that seizures and mental illness are illnesses, to be treated with medicine and care, and that it is wrong and harmful to tell a sick person they have a demon. The Gospels themselves know the difference.

The father says his son was thrown into fire and water to kill him. If you, or someone you love, are at risk of harm, reach for real help now: a doctor, a pastor you trust, or a crisis line in your country. Jesus did not leave this boy alone, and you are not meant to face such danger alone.

Some Bibles add 'and fasting' to verse 29. Two of the oldest copies, Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, do not have those words, and most modern Bibles leave them out. Many scholars think they were added later.
passages.asks: The father's prayer is one of the most honest in the Bible. He has some faith and knows it is not enough, and he asks Jesus to help with both. You do not need perfect faith to come. Ask whether you can pray his prayer: I believe; help my unbelief.

passages.happening: Jesus travels quietly through Galilee, teaching his disciples. He tells them a second time that the Son of Man will be handed over, killed, and after three days rise. They do not understand and are afraid to ask. At Capernaum he asks what they were arguing about on the road. They say nothing, because they had been arguing about which of them was the greatest. Jesus sits down, calls the Twelve, and says that whoever wants to be first must be last of all and servant of all. Then he takes a little child in his arms. Whoever welcomes a child like this in his name, he says, welcomes him, and welcomes the one who sent him.
passages.hearers:
Teachers sat to teach, as Jesus did in the synagogue at Nazareth (Luke 4:20). Mark notes that Jesus 'sat down'. What follows is a lesson, not a passing remark.

A small child had no power and could offer nothing in return. Greek even used the same word, pais, for a child and for a servant. To welcome a child gained a man nothing. It brought no honour.

The contrast is sharp. Jesus has just said he will be handed over to die. The disciples, walking behind him, argue about rank. Mark does not soften it.
passages.ot: Jesus will soon say plainly why he came: “For even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45). The servant of Isaiah, who is despised and rejected (Isaiah 53:3), stands behind both his words about dying and his words about serving.
passages.asks: The disciples went quiet when Jesus asked what they had been discussing. They knew. Ask what you would rather Jesus did not overhear: your plans for your own importance, your comparisons with others. And ask who, in your circle, is like that child, someone who can do nothing for you, and how you might welcome them.

passages.happening: John tells Jesus that they saw a man driving out demons in Jesus' name, and they tried to stop him because he was not one of their group. Jesus says, “Do not stop him.” No one who does a mighty work in his name will soon speak against him. Whoever is not against us is for us. Even someone who gives you a cup of water because you belong to Christ will not lose his reward.
passages.hearers:
Using powerful names to drive out spirits was common in the ancient world. Acts tells of Jewish exorcists in Ephesus who tried to use Jesus' name without knowing him, saying, “I bind you by Jesus, whom Paul proclaims” (Acts 19:13). It went badly for them. The man John reports seems different. He is actually freeing people in Jesus' name.

There is a sting here. Just a few verses earlier the disciples themselves failed to drive out a spirit (9:18). Now they want to stop someone who succeeded.

A cup of water was the smallest kindness in a hot land. Jesus says even that, given to his people, counts with God.
passages.ot: Something like this happened to Moses. Two men began to prophesy outside the camp, and Joshua said, “Moses, my lord, stop them!” Moses answered, “Are you jealous on my account? I wish that all the LORD’s people were prophets” (Numbers 11:28-29).
passages.hard: Elsewhere Jesus says, “He who is not with Me is against Me” (Matthew 12:30). Do the two sayings clash? They answer different situations. In Matthew, Jesus speaks of those who oppose his work and call it the devil's. Here, he speaks of someone doing good in his name, though not in the disciples' circle. One saying warns against standing on the fence about Jesus. The other warns against drawing the circle around ourselves.
passages.asks: John's complaint was that the man 'does not follow us'. Not 'does not follow you'. Ask where you treat your own church, group, or tradition as the line of God's work, and whether there are people serving Jesus whom you have been slow to welcome.

passages.happening: Jesus warns that it would be better to be thrown into the sea with a great millstone round your neck than to cause one of these little ones who believe in him to stumble. Then he says that if your hand, your foot, or your eye causes you to sin, cut it off or pluck it out. It is better to enter life maimed than to be thrown whole into hell, where “their worm never dies, and the fire is never quenched.” Everyone will be salted with fire. Salt is good, but if it loses its saltiness, nothing can restore it. So have salt among yourselves, and be at peace with one another.
passages.hearers:
The millstone Jesus names is literally a 'donkey millstone', the large upper stone of a mill that needed a donkey to turn it. A household hand mill was small. This was a huge stone. Tied to a neck, it meant certain drowning.

The word Jesus uses for hell is Gehenna. It comes from the Hebrew name of the Valley of Hinnom, a real valley beside Jerusalem. There, in the worst days of Judah, people had burned their own children as sacrifices to false gods (Jeremiah 7:31). Jeremiah said it would be called “the Valley of Slaughter” (Jeremiah 7:32). Over time its name became a word for the place of God's final judgment. You may hear that Gehenna was a burning rubbish dump. That idea first appears in a Jewish commentator around AD 1200, and there is no ancient evidence for it.

Salt kept food from going bad and gave it flavour. In Israel's worship every grain offering had to be seasoned with salt, “the salt of the covenant of your God” (Leviticus 2:13).
passages.ot: The words about the worm and the fire are the very last words of Isaiah: “their worm will never die, their fire will never be quenched” (Isaiah 66:24). Isaiah's book ends with a new heaven and earth, and with this warning beside it.
passages.hard:
Does Jesus want people to cut off their hands or put out their eyes? No. He is using a strong picture, as teachers in his culture often did, to show how serious sin is. The point is to cut off whatever leads you into sin, a habit, a place, a relationship, a screen, however much it costs. The church has always taught that this is not a command to harm the body. If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, please speak to someone now: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line.

'Everyone will be salted with fire' (verse 49) is one of the hardest verses in Mark, and there is no agreed reading. Some think of the salt on every offering (Leviticus 2:13), so that disciples are offerings made pure through testing and suffering. Others think of the fire of judgment. It is wise to hold the meaning loosely.

On hell itself, Christians agree that Jesus warned of real and final judgment. They differ on what that judgment is like, and these notes do not settle that here.
passages.asks: Jesus speaks most fiercely about those who make the weak stumble. Ask whether anything in your life, your words, your example, your anger, makes it harder for someone young in faith to trust Jesus. And ask what you need to cut off, not from your body but from your habits, to keep walking with him.
